title: The Oliver date that was really for Clarence Williams
summary: Williams, who Bigard calls a big crook who stole 'Sister Kate' from Piron, could not get Buster Bailey and got Bigard to record on a date he thought was Oliver's.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Well, after you joined Duke and then you recorded with King Oliver, who else recorded with King Oliver at that time? That was in '27 or '28.

He had to pick up men from around New York and -- oh, I think there was a little trombone player I used to know real well. I can't think of his name offhand, so skip him. But it was nothing. It was all Clarence Williams' tunes.

You see, I was kind of ornery, too, at times. Clarence Williams, he knew I wasn't working when I got to New York and he gave all the time he wanted a clarinet player, he got Buster Bailey. So then when he couldn't get -- and he knew I was in town and he knew I was from New Orleans, too. And he was a big crook, Clarence Williams.

So, finally, anyway, he couldn't get Buster -- Buster would be working -- and he tried to get me and I wouldn't go. So he was telling King Oliver to talk to me to record and I still wouldn't go in. And the only way I recorded, which I didn't know until afterwards, I thought it was King Oliver's date but it was for Clarence Williams, see?

And that Clarence Williams was a big crook. He stole 'Sister Kate' from A. J. Piron, till Piron got wise and they was going to stick him in jail and he came up with all that back money that he owed Piron. So that's the way it went.
